Learning Objectives
Assess the foundation behind patient safety.
Identify the importance of communication between physicians and patients to limit patient
grievances.
Define the key components of medical malpractice.
Implement appropriate checklists to prevent medical errors.
Key Terms
Abandonment: termination of the physician-patient relationship by the physician without
reasonable notice to the patient at a time when the patient requires medical attention and
without the opportunity to plan for appropriate continuation and follow-up care

Burden of proof: typically, the plaintiff’s responsibility to affirmatively prove a fact or facts in
dispute on an issue raised between parties in a case
Causation: The causal connection between the act or omission of the defendant and the
injury suffered by the plaintiff; the plaintiff must show causation of an injury by the defendant
to prove negligence.
Damages: Money receivable through judicial order by a plaintiff who sustained harm,
impairment, or loss to his or her person or property as the result of the accidental, intentional,
or negligent act of another; damages can be grouped into two primary types: compensatory
and punitive.
Compensatory damages compensate the injured party for the injury sustained and nothing
more. Compensatory damages can be divided into economic, noneconomic, and special
damages.
Economic damages include an estimate of the lost wages, both past and future, of the
plaintiff and affected family members and all costs associated with the residual disability of
the patient.
Noneconomic damages include intangible damage resulting from the negligent act, such as
pain and suffering, disfigurement, and interference with the ordinary enjoyment of life.
Special damages are the actual out-of-pocket losses incurred by the plaintiff, such as
medical expenses, rehabilitation expenses, and earnings lost during treatment and
recovery.
Punitive damages are awarded to punish a defendant who has acted maliciously or in
reckless disregard of the plaintiff’s rights.
Duty: the obligation of the physician to care for the patient in a manner that is consistent with
the quality of care provided by other physicians in treating a patient’s particular condition
Fraud: the intentional deception or misrepresentation that an individual knows to be false or
does not believe to be true and makes, knowing that the deception may result in some
unauthorized benefit to himself or herself or to some other person
Informed consent: Consent is fully informed only if the patient knows and understands the
information necessary to make an informed decision about the treatment or procedure. No
informed consent exists if the treatment or procedure extends beyond the scope of consent.
For example, if the risk associated with the changed treatment or procedure is substantially
different from that contemplated by the patient, the courts may find that the original informed
consent was not sufficient. The circumstances in which special informed consent rules apply
are medical emergencies, situations involving a minor, and rare circumstances in which
authorization for a treatment or procedure is obtained from a court.

Malpractice: in the case of a physician, failure to exercise the degree of care and skill that a
physician or surgeon of the same specialty would use under similar circumstances
(professional negligence); care below the standard of care
Negligence: in medical malpractice cases, a legal cause of action involving the failure of a
defendant physician to exercise the degree of diligence and care that an average qualified
physician practicing in the same specialty as that of the defendant physician would have
exercised in a similar situation and that has resulted in the breach of a legal duty owed by the
physician to the patient that proximately caused an injury that the law recognizes as deserving
of compensation (damages)
Res ipsa loquitur (The thing speaks for itself): A doctrine that may be invoked in a negligence
action if the plaintiff has no direct evidence of negligence but the injury itself results in the
inference that it would not have occurred in the absence of a negligent act. It raises an
inference of the defendant’s negligence, thereby altering the burden of proof so that the
defendant must produce evidence that he or she did not commit a negligent act.
Physician impairment: the inability or impending inability to practice within the accepted
standard of care as a result of substance use, abuse, dependency, or addiction
Medicolegal Issues
Patient Safety and Medical Errors
In 1996, the Institute of Medicine launched a concerted, ongoing effort focused on assessing
and improving the nation’s quality of care. This consists of three phases, which recognize the
issue of quality, the need for improvement, and the implementation of reform (Video 1).
First phase (1996 to 1998)—Documented the serious and pervasive nature of the nation’s
overall quality problem, concluding that “the burden of harm conveyed by the collective
impact of all of our health care quality problems is staggering.”
Second phase (1999 to 2001)—The Committee on Quality of Health Care in America released
two reports, establishing a vision for how the healthcare system and related policy
environment must be transformed radically.
To Err Is Human: Building a Safer Health System (1999) reported that tens of thousands of
Americans die each year as a result of medical errors. It highlighted the importance of
patient safety and quality issues for public and private policymakers.
Crossing the Quality Chasm: A New Health System for the 21st Century (2001) stressed broader
quality issues and described six aims of care: safety, effectiveness, patient-centeredness,

Collaborative Efforts
The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality is the research arm of the US
Department of Health and Human Services and the sister agency to the National
Institutes of Health. As the home to specialized research centers in major areas of
healthcare research, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality focuses on quality
improvement in patient safety by identifying factors that put patients at risk, the
development of innovative approaches that reduce errors and produce safety in various
healthcare settings and geographically diverse locations, the dissemination of research
results, and the improvement of patient safety education and training for clinicians and
other providers. In doing so, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality also
assesses outcomes and the effectiveness of care as well as healthcare costs and sources
of payment. The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality supports research on
health disparities, drugs and other therapeutics, primary care practice, and integrated
healthcare delivery systems and focuses on evidence-based practice and the translation
of research into clinical practice to improve patient care in diverse healthcare settings.
Lastly, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality identifies strategies to improve
healthcare access, foster appropriate use, and reduce unnecessary expenditures.
The Joint Commission is the major accrediting agency for hospitals. In 1996, it developed
a sentinel reporting policy that encourages accredited healthcare organizations to
voluntarily report a sentinel event, defined as “an unexpected occurrence involving
death or serious physical or psychological injury, or the risk thereof,” within 5 days and
to submit a root cause analysis within 45 days of discovery. Serious injury specifically
includes a loss of limb or function. The phrase “the risk thereof” includes the risk of
recurrence of any process variations that would be associated with a considerable risk of
a serious adverse outcome. Based on root cause analyses, the Joint Commission
identified the need to establish national patient safety goals, and the first goals were
established in 2002. The Joint Commission re-evaluates these patient safety goals
annually and identifies steps every year to accomplish the goals. It allows alternatives to
specific recommendations if the alternative is as effective as the original
recommendation in achieving the specific patient safety goal.

The Joint Commission identified 15 National Patient Safety Goals. Each year, specific
steps are identified to accomplish the overarching goals. One example of a goal or step
that is specific to orthopaedics includes Goal No. 1 of the Joint Commission 2013
National Patient Safety Goals, which is to improve the accuracy of patient identification
with the elimination of wrong-site surgery. This involves the use of the American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Sign Your Site program, which requires a pre-
procedure time-out to confirm the correct patient, procedure, and site via active
communication techniques. Another example is Goal No. 7 of the Joint Commission 2013
National Patient Safety Goals, which was set to reduce the risk of healthcare-associated
infections. This requires healthcare organizations to establish systems to ensure that the
use of prophylactic antibiotic agents for total hip arthroplasty, total knee arthroplasty,
and hip fracture management adheres to the best available evidence, including
appropriate antibiotic agent selection, administration of the antibiotic agent within 60
minutes of the surgical incision, and discontinuation of prophylactic antibiotic therapy
within 24 hours of wound closure.
The National Patient Safety Foundation consists of stakeholders that include healthcare
practitioners and institutions, manufacturers, educators, insurers, researchers, legal
advisers, policymakers, and patients. The mission of the National Patient Safety
Foundation is to identify a core body of knowledge, identify pathways to apply
knowledge, develop and enhance the culture of receptivity to patient safety, and raise
public awareness and foster communications about patient safety.
Patient Safety

Patient Safety
Wrong-site surgery prevention involves preoperative surgical site marking and the
introduction of a surgical time-out, abiding to the Joint Commission and the World
Health Organization surgical safety checklists to identify members of the surgical team
and to ensure the correct surgical site, procedure, and location.

Compliance

Compliance
Resource 1 provides insight into five important federal fraud and abuse laws, including
the Stark Laws, that all physicians must be aware of. Rationale for prohibitions may
include excessive medical services that were ordered for which a patient received
unnecessary care, resulting in higher healthcare costs or costs for patients covered by
government programs that ultimately were passed on to taxpayers. Stark Law I (1989)
prohibits the referral of Medicare patients who need clinical laboratory services to
entities in which the physician has an ownership interest; prohibits the referral of
Medicare and certain Medicaid patients for designated health services to entities in
which the physician or an immediate family member has a financial interest, unless an
exemption applies; and proscribes entities to which referrals are made from submitting
payment claims to the government for specified services. Stark Law II (1993) expands the
list of referral services that are prohibited from physician ownership; expands the
referral ban to include patients covered by certain Medicaid-managed care programs;
and identifies circumstances under which referrals are considered permitted activities,
known as exceptions. Final regulations for the enactment of Stark Law II (1998) were
rolled out in two phases, superseded the 1995 Stark Law I regulations, and consisted of
actual rules physicians must follow. Penalties for violating Stark Law II (phases I and II)
regulations include denial of payment, mandatory refunding of payments that were
made in error, civil monetary penalties of $15,000 per claim, or prohibition from
participation in Medicare and Medicaid programs. Phase II exceptions include five
important factors that are relevant to orthopaedic surgeons: in-office ancillary services in
a group practice or by a sole practitioner, bona fide employment, personal service
arrangements, fair market value compensation, and academic medical centers.

Resource 2 provides information on the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability
Act and serves as a reference for patients and professionals. Title I protects health
insurance coverage for workers and their families if the workers change or lose their
jobs. Title II addresses administrative simplification, as well as fraud, abuse, and medical
liability reform. Title III establishes medical savings accounts and health insurance
deductions for the self-employed. Title IV covers the enforcement of group health plan
provisions. Title V focuses on revenue offset provisions.
Privacy rules create national standards to protect patient medical records and other
personal health information; give patients more control over their health data; limit the
way healthcare providers may use the information and release it to third parties;
establish guidelines that must be followed to protect the privacy of a patient’s protected
health information; and hold health plans, healthcare clearinghouses, and healthcare
providers accountable for violations.
Fraud

Fraud
According to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, “fraud is the intentional
deception or misrepresentation that an individual knows to be false or does not believe
to be true and makes, knowing that the deception could result in some unauthorized
benefit to himself/herself or some other person. The most frequent kind of fraud arises
from a false statement or misrepresentation made, or caused to be made, that is
material to entitlement or payment under the Medicare program.” The most common
types of fraud in Medicare are billing for services not rendered (ie, coding for procedures
not supported by the clinical documentation); performing services not medically
necessary; misrepresenting a diagnosis to justify payment; soliciting, offering, or
receiving a kickback; unbundling; falsifying treatment plans and medical records to
justify payment; and upcoding (ie, altering diagnosis or treatment codes to increase
reimbursement).

Medical Malpractice Claims

Medical Malpractice Claims
A patient must prove certain elements in a malpractice claim. These include duty of care,
breach of duty, harm, and causation. The duty of care, or a physician’s obligation to care
for a patient, should be consistent with the quality of care provided by other physicians
in treating a patient’s particular condition The breach of duty are facts that demonstrate
a physician failed to meet the standard of care in treating a patient. This may occur via
an act or omission, leading to patient injury. A poor outcome, permanent or not, or a
predictable complication does not necessarily mean that a physician has deviated from
the standard of care. Causation is proof that a violation caused a patient’s injury,
whereas damage is proof that a physician’s deviation from the standard of care resulted
in physical, emotional, or financial injury to a patient (Video 2).


Informed Consent
Informed consent requires that a physician obtain consent before rendering any
treatment, performing any surgical procedure, and performing certain diagnostic
procedures (Video 3). Treating physicians must disclose to the patient who will be
performing the surgical procedure and explain the procedure at the patient’s level of
understanding and in the patient’s native language (an interpreter may be necessary). In
addition, surgical implants must be disclosed to the patient during the informed consent
process. Informed consent has implications for patients of certain religious backgrounds
and for animal-based implants, such as bovine-based products. In addition, a patient
must give permission before being touched by another person. Without permission,
contact may be considered an assault, a battery, or a trespass on the patient. Without an
informed consent, an orthopaedic physician may be held liable for violation of a patient’s
rights, regardless whether the treatment was appropriate and rendered with due care.
Medical care cannot be provided without expressed or implied permission for the
physician to act. In the emergent surgical management of a life-threatening injury, the
surgeon should confirm the necessity of the surgical procedure with another
orthopaedic surgeon.

Patient Grievances

Patient Grievances
Factors that increase the likelihood of a suit and successful prosecution of medical
malpractice claims include miscommunication, delayed response to patient or family
concerns, failure to diagnose, failure to treat, and improper treatment. Factors that
contribute to patient grievances include inconsistent communication, unkept promises,
lack of sufficient details about diagnoses and treatment plans, perceived rudeness, and
lack of understanding of procedural and surgical complications. Other factors may
include the perception that the physician and staff are too busy to be concerned with the
patient’s problem, long wait times, or inability to resolve a painful condition.
Effective patient-physician communication may avert many patient grievances. Empathy
is a key trait that all physicians should embrace within the patient-physician relationship.
Some tools that may be used to provide high-quality patient-physician communication
include providing the patient with adequate time, acknowledging emotional distress,
paying attention and listening to the details of patient concerns, and returning phone
calls in a timely fashion. Strategies to address grievances when first expressed include
taking all grievances seriously; acknowledging the patient’s concern or report; providing
accurate information to help clarify the situation; being honest, open, and transparent;
avoiding negative comments about other healthcare providers; and providing clear and
succinct status updates.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services require all grievances to be addressed
with a written response to the patient in a timely manner. Situations requiring a written
response to a patient may include a specific request by a patient for a written report or a
dispute about charges based on a patient’s perception of the quality of care.
Components of the written response may include acknowledgment of the report,

Standard of Disclosure

Standard of Disclosure
The standard of disclosure varies by state. Two standards for assessing the adequacy of
disclosure are the professional or reasonable physicians’ standard (which is based on
what is customary practice in the medical community for physicians to divulge to
patients) and the patient viewpoint standard (which is based on what a reasonable
person in the patient’s position would want to know in similar circumstances).
Elements of Informed Consent

Elements of Informed Consent
Components of informed consent include stating the diagnosis, the nature of the
condition or illness requiring medical or surgical management, the nature and purpose
of the treatment option or the recommended procedure, the risks and potential
complications associated with the recommended treatment option or procedure, all the
feasible alternative treatment options or procedures (including the option of taking no
action), and the relative probability of the success of the treatment option or procedures
in terms the patient will understand.
